Drunk
drungk
v. and adj. (past participle of drink; overcome with strong drink)
Past participle of drink, Saxon drincan. The Authorized Version uses the word both innocently — men who have eaten and drunk — and morally, and it is one of the few sins Scripture illustrates chiefly by showing what it did to particular men on particular nights.

Biblical Definition

“And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). Paul sets the two fillings against each other, and the contrast tells us what drunkenness actually is: a man surrendering the governance of himself to something, and the question is only to what. Scripture then shows the ruin in cases. David “made him drunk” (2Sa 11:13) — the king could not get Uriah to go down to his own house sober, so he tried it with wine, and when even a drunk Uriah kept faith with the ark and the army in the field, David wrote the letter. Elah was “drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza” when Zimri killed him (1Ki 16:9); Benhadad and thirty-two kings were “drinking themselves drunk in the pavilions” at noon on the day their army was broken (1Ki 20:16). Belshazzar drank wine out of the vessels of the LORD's house and praised gods of silver and gold, and the hand wrote on the wall that night (Dan 5:23). The word also carries the wrath of God in a fearful figure: “I will make mine arrows drunk with blood” (Deu 32:42), and Jerusalem “hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury” (Isa 51:17) — the cup our Lord took at Gethsemane and drained.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines drunk as intoxicated, inebriated; and adds the Scriptural sense of being drenched or saturated — as arrows made drunk with blood.

expand to see more

DRUNK, a. Intoxicated; inebriated with strong liquor.

1. Drenched or saturated with moisture or liquor. I will make my arrows drunk with blood. Deuteronomy 32.

DRUNKENNESS, n. Intoxication; inebriation; a state in which a person is overwhelmed or overpowered with spirituous liquors.

2. Disorder of the faculties resembling intoxication by liquors; inflammation; frenzy; rage.

Key Scripture

Eph 5:18 — "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;"

2Sa 11:13 — "And when David had called him, he did eat and drink before him; and he made him drunk: and at even he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but went not down to his house."

Dan 5:23 — "But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know: and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified:"

Isa 51:17 — "Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out."

Modern Corruption

Drunkenness has been reclassified as a disease and thereby moved out of the category Scripture puts it in.

expand to see more

The dominant modern account treats drunkenness as an illness with a sufferer rather than a sin with a sinner, and the pastoral consequence is that repentance is no longer the remedy offered. Scripture is not naive about bondage — it says plainly that whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin, and the misery of the habitual drunkard is real and deep. But 1 Corinthians 6:10 lists drunkards among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God, and then adds the sentence that no disease model can supply: and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified. A category that cannot be repented of cannot be forgiven, and a man told he has only a condition has been robbed of the only door out.

The opposite error is the teetotal absolutism that treats wine itself as evil, which Scripture will not support: it gives wine to make glad the heart of man, our Lord made it at Cana, and Paul told Timothy to use a little for his stomach's sake. The line the Bible draws is not at the cup but at the surrender — wherein is excess. A believer may abstain wholly, and there is much wisdom in it where a conscience is weak or a brother is stumbled; but he abstains as a matter of liberty and love, not because Scripture has forbidden what it blessed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shakar (H7937), to be or become drunk; shikkor (H7910), a drunkard; Greek methusko (G3182), to be intoxicated; asotia (G810), excess, riot.

expand to see more

Hebrew shakar (H7937) — to drink to the full, to become drunk; 2 Samuel 11:13, Deuteronomy 32:42.

Hebrew shathah (H8354) — to drink; the ordinary verb, morally neutral in itself.

Greek methusko (G3182) — to make drunk, to be intoxicated; Ephesians 5:18, Luke 12:45.

Greek asotia (G810) — unsavedness, riot, excess, dissipation; Ephesians 5:18, the state wine is here said to hold.

Greek pleroo (G4137) — to be filled; the imperative set against being drunk — be being filled with the Spirit.

Usage

"“Be not drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” — two governances, one man."

"“He made him drunk” — and Uriah still would not go home."

"“Drinking himself drunk in the pavilions” — at noon, thirty-two kings."
